title: Pinasugbo
intro: Long, thin strips of saba fried until crisp, then coated in brown sugar caramel and sprinkled with toasted sesame seeds. Crunchy, sweet and nutty, like banana brittle.

steps.text: Slice each banana lengthwise into strips about 5 mm (1/4 in) thick.
Heat the oil in a wok to 170°C (340°F). Fry the strips in batches until golden and crisp at the edges. Drain on a rack.
Pour off all but a thin film of oil. Add the brown sugar and water and stir over medium heat until the sugar melts and bubbles into a syrup.
Return the fried bananas to the pan and toss quickly until coated. Sprinkle with the sesame seeds while the caramel is wet.
Spread the strips apart on a greased tray or banana leaf and let them cool until the caramel hardens.

tips: Store in an airtight container once fully cool and eat within 2 days. Humid air softens the caramel, so keep the lid on.

title: Banana chips
intro: Thin rounds of barely ripe saba, fried until crisp and glazed with a light sugar syrup that dries to a sweet, crackly coating. A crunchy snack that keeps for days.

items.name: saba bananas
items.note: green to just turning yellow, peeled

steps.text: Slice the bananas thinly, about 2 mm, on a slight diagonal. A mandoline makes it quick and even. Drop the slices into a bowl of water as you go so they do not darken.
Drain and pat the slices very dry with towels.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to 170°C (340°F). Fry in small batches, stirring, until golden and the bubbling slows. Drain on a rack.
In a wide pan, boil the sugar, water and salt until it thickens into a syrup that coats a spoon.
Take the pan off the heat, add the fried chips and toss until evenly glazed.
Spread the chips out on a tray in one layer and let them cool and dry until the coating is hard.

tips: Greener bananas give crisper chips; ripe ones turn chewy. Store the cooled chips in an airtight jar for up to a week.

title: Kamote chips
intro: Paper-thin slices of sweet potato fried until crisp and lightly sweet, finished with salt or a dusting of sugar. Crunchy, golden and easy to snack on by the handful.

steps.text: Slice the sweet potatoes very thinly, about 2 mm, with a mandoline or sharp knife.
Soak the slices in cold water to rinse off surface starch, which helps them crisp.
Drain and dry the slices thoroughly between towels. Wet slices spatter and turn soggy.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to 165°C (330°F). Fry in small batches, stirring, until golden and the bubbling almost stops.
Lift onto a rack and season right away with salt or sugar. They crisp more as they cool.

tips: Sweet potatoes burn quickly because of their sugar, so pull the chips out when they are light gold, not brown.

title: Camote fries
intro: Sweet potato sticks fried twice so they come out crisp outside and soft inside, tossed with salt or sugar. Good with banana ketchup or a garlicky mayo dip.

steps.text: Cut the sweet potatoes into sticks about 1 cm (1/2 in) thick. Soak in cold water to rinse off starch.
Drain, pat very dry and toss with the cornstarch until lightly coated.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to 165°C (330°F). Fry in batches until soft and just starting to color. Drain on a rack.
Raise the oil to 190°C (375°F). Fry the sticks again in batches until crisp and golden.
Drain and toss with salt or sugar while hot. Serve with banana ketchup.

tips: Fries can be done through the first fry an hour ahead; keep them on the rack and do the second fry just before serving.

title: Nilagang kamote
intro: Whole sweet potatoes boiled in their skins until soft and steaming, peeled at the table and eaten plain or with a little butter and sugar. A warm, filling afternoon snack with coffee.

steps.text: Put the sweet potatoes in a pot, cut any very large ones in half, and cover with water. Add the salt.
Bring to a boil, then lower the heat, cover and simmer until a knife slides into the center easily.
Drain and leave the pot uncovered on the turned-off burner so the surface dries a little.
Serve warm, peeling as you eat, with butter or sugar if you like.

tips: Pick sweet potatoes of the same thickness so they cook evenly. Leftovers are good fried in butter the next morning.

title: Nilagang kamoteng kahoy
intro: Cassava boiled until tender and slightly translucent, then served warm with freshly grated coconut and sugar. Dense, mildly sweet and satisfying.

steps.text: Cut the cassava into 10 cm (4 in) pieces. Slit the skin lengthwise and peel off both the brown bark and the pink layer underneath. Rinse well.
Halve thick pieces lengthwise and pull out the woody string in the center.
Cover with water in a pot, add the salt and bring to a boil. Simmer uncovered until the cassava is fork tender and some pieces begin to split.
Drain well. Serve warm, topped with grated coconut and a sprinkle of sugar.

tips: Cassava must always be peeled and fully cooked, never eaten raw. Buy the sweet kind sold for cooking, boil it in plenty of water and throw out any pieces that stay hard or taste bitter.

title: Shrimp and squash okoy
intro: Lacy fritters of shredded squash and small whole shrimp, fried until crisp and dipped in spiced vinegar. Crunchy at the edges, sweet from the squash and savory from the shrimp.

items.name: small shrimp
items.note: heads and legs trimmed, shells on

items.name: squash (kalabasa)
items.note: peeled and cut into thin matchsticks

steps.text: Mix the vinegar, garlic, onion, chili and salt and set aside.
Whisk the flour, cornstarch, egg, cold water, fish sauce, salt and pepper into a thin batter.
Add the squash, green onions and half the shrimp and fold until everything is lightly coated. The batter should just bind the vegetables, not drown them.
Heat about 1.5 cm (1/2 in) of oil in a frying pan to 175°C (350°F).
Spoon in about 1/4 cup of the mixture per fritter and flatten it with the back of the spoon. Press 2 or 3 of the remaining shrimp on top.
Fry until the bottom is golden and crisp, then flip and fry the other side.
Drain on a rack and serve hot with the spiced vinegar.

tips: Keep the batter cold and thin for a lacy, crisp okoy. Thick batter makes heavy, bready fritters.

title: Ukoy with togue
intro: Crisp, flat fritters of mung bean sprouts topped with tiny shrimp, fried on a saucer-shaped base so they keep their round shape. Crunchy and light, with a garlicky vinegar dip.

steps.text: Stir together the vinegar, garlic, salt and pepper for the dip.
Whisk the rice flour, flour, baking powder, annatto, salt, egg and cold water into a smooth, pourable batter.
Heat about 2 cm (3/4 in) of oil in a frying pan to 175°C (350°F).
Pile a handful of bean sprouts on a small saucer or a flat ladle. Spoon about 3 tablespoons of batter over them and scatter a few shrimp on top.
Lower the saucer to the oil and tip the fritter in, or hold the ladle in the oil until the fritter sets and slides off. Fry until golden underneath, then flip.
Fry the second side until crisp, drain on a rack and serve hot with the dip.

tips: Dry the bean sprouts well after rinsing; any water on them makes the oil spit and the fritters soft.

title: Ilocos empanada
intro: A thin, crisp orange rice-flour shell folded around shredded green papaya, garlicky longganisa and a whole egg, deep-fried and doused with spiced cane vinegar. Crunchy, savory and very filling.

steps.text: Mix all the dip ingredients and set aside.
For the dough, mix the rice flour, flour, salt and annatto. Add the warm water and oil and knead to a smooth, soft dough like clay. Cover and rest.
Toss the papaya with the salt and leave it while the dough rests, then squeeze out as much liquid as you can.
Crumble the longganisa into a dry pan and cook over medium heat, stirring, until browned and cooked through. Drain off the fat.
Divide the dough into 6 balls. Roll each between two oiled sheets of plastic or banana leaf into a circle about 18 cm (7 in) across and 2 mm thick.
Peel off the top sheet. Spread 1/2 cup of papaya on one half of the circle, make a well in the middle, add a sixth of the longganisa and crack an egg into the well.
Using the bottom sheet, fold the empty half over the filling. Press the edges together and trim them neatly with the rim of a saucer.
Heat the oil in a wide, deep pan to 175°C (350°F). Slide in one or two empanadas and fry, spooning oil over the top, until the shell is crisp and orange-gold and the egg is set.
Drain on a rack and serve hot, cut open, with the vinegar dip poured over or on the side.

tips: If the dough cracks when you fold it, knead in a spoonful more warm water. A handful of mung bean sprouts mixed into the papaya is a common addition.

title: Batangas empanada
intro: Large fried turnovers with a crisp, flaky crust and a savory filling of ground beef and potato. Usually eaten with a sharp, garlicky vinegar for dipping.

items.name: large potato
items.note: peeled and cut into small dice

items.name: spiced vinegar
items.note: cane vinegar with plenty of garlic and onion

steps.text: For the dough, mix the flour, sugar and salt. Rub in the butter with your fingers until it looks like coarse crumbs.
Beat the egg with the cold water, add it to the flour and mix just until it holds together. Wrap and chill.
For the filling, sauté the garlic and onion in the oil until soft. Add the beef and cook, breaking it up, until browned.
Add the potato, soy sauce, water, sugar, salt and pepper. Cover and simmer until the potato is tender and the pan is nearly dry. Stir in the raisins and let the filling cool completely.
Roll the dough out on a floured surface to about 3 mm thick and cut out 15 cm (6 in) circles, rerolling the scraps.
Put about 3 tablespoons of filling on one half of each circle. Brush the edge with water, fold over and press closed, then crimp with a fork.
Heat the oil in a deep pot to 170°C (340°F). Fry 2 or 3 at a time, turning, until deep golden and crisp.
Drain on a rack and serve warm with the spiced vinegar.

tips: Make sure the filling is cold before you fill the dough, or the butter melts and the crust turns tough. Shaped, unfried empanadas freeze well for a month.

title: Chicken empanada
intro: Baked half-moon pastries with a buttery crust and a slightly sweet filling of chicken, potato, carrot, peas and raisins. A favorite for afternoon snacks and packed lunches.

steps.text: For the dough, whisk the flour, sugar and salt. Rub in the butter until only pea-sized pieces remain.
Mix the egg yolk with the cold water, add it and stir with a fork just until the dough comes together. Flatten into a disc, wrap and chill.
For the filling, sauté the garlic and onion in the oil until soft. Add the chicken and cook until it is no longer pink.
Add the potato, carrot, soy sauce and water. Cover and simmer until the vegetables are tender and most of the liquid is gone.
Stir in the peas, raisins, sugar, salt and pepper and cook 2 minutes more. Spread on a plate and let it cool completely.
Heat the oven to 200°C (400°F) and line a baking sheet with parchment.
Roll the dough about 3 mm thick and cut 12 circles of 12 cm (5 in). Fill each with 2 heaped tablespoons of filling, fold, seal with water and crimp the edge with a fork.
Arrange on the sheet, brush with the egg wash and poke a small hole in each top for steam.
Bake until deep golden.
Cool on the sheet for 10 minutes before serving; the filling is very hot.

tips: These also fry well: fry the shaped empanadas at 170°C (340°F) for about 5 minutes and skip the egg wash.

title: Ngohiong
intro: Spring rolls filled with heart of palm, pork and shrimp, fragrant with five-spice, dipped in a thin batter and fried crisp. Served with a sweet, sticky chili sauce.

items.name: ubod (heart of palm)
items.note: fresh or canned, cut into thin strips; or singkamas

steps.text: Sauté the garlic and onion in the oil until soft. Add the pork and cook, breaking it up, until no longer pink.
Add the shrimp, ubod, carrot, five-spice, soy sauce, salt and pepper and cook until the shrimp turn pink and the vegetables soften. Drain off liquid and let the filling cool.
For the sauce, simmer the water, brown sugar, soy sauce, garlic and chilies. Stir in the cornstarch mixture and cook until thick and glossy.
Place 2 heaped tablespoons of filling near one corner of each wrapper, fold in the sides and roll up tightly. Seal with a dab of water.
Whisk the batter ingredients until smooth. Heat the oil in a deep pot to 175°C (350°F).
Dip each roll in the batter, let the extra drip off and fry in batches, turning, until crisp and golden.
Drain on a rack and serve hot with the sauce, whole or cut in half on the diagonal.

tips: Canned hearts of palm are a good stand-in for fresh ubod; rinse and squeeze them dry first.

title: Cheese sticks
intro: Sticks of quick-melt cheese wrapped in lumpia wrappers and fried until shatteringly crisp, with soft, melted cheese inside. A party and after-school snack, great with banana ketchup or sweet chili sauce.

items.name: quick-melt cheese
items.note: cut into 20 sticks about 1 x 1 x 8 cm

items.name: all-purpose flour
items.note: mixed with 1 tbsp water, for sealing

items.name: banana ketchup or sweet chili sauce

steps.text: Lay a wrapper like a diamond and put a cheese stick across the bottom corner.
Fold the corner over, fold in both sides and roll up tightly. Seal the tip with the flour paste. Repeat with the rest.
Freeze the rolls on a tray so the cheese firms up and does not leak.
Heat the oil in a pan to 175°C (350°F). Fry in batches, turning, until golden and crisp. Pull them out as soon as they color.
Drain on a rack and serve hot with banana ketchup or sweet chili sauce.

tips: Wrap with two layers of wrapper if yours are very thin, and make sure there are no gaps at the ends: that is where cheese escapes.

title: Dynamite lumpia
intro: Long green chilies stuffed with seasoned ground pork and a strip of cheese, wrapped in lumpia wrappers and fried until crisp. Mildly hot, savory and gooey, with a sweet-creamy dip.

steps.text: Wearing gloves, slit each chili lengthwise on one side, leaving the stem on, and scrape out the seeds and white ribs.
Sauté the garlic and onion in the oil until soft. Add the pork, soy sauce, salt and pepper and cook, breaking it up, until browned and cooked through. Let it cool.
Fill each chili with a little of the pork and tuck in a strip of cheese. Press the chili closed around the filling.
Roll each chili tightly in a wrapper, leaving the stem sticking out of one end. Seal with a dab of water.
Heat the oil in a pan to 175°C (350°F). Fry in batches, turning, until the wrappers are golden and crisp.
Drain on a rack. Mix the mayonnaise and ketchup and serve with the hot lumpia.

tips: Scraping out all the seeds and ribs keeps the heat mild. For a meatless version, fill the chilies with cheese only.

title: Homemade chicharon
intro: Pork skin boiled, scraped, dried until glassy and then fried so it puffs into light, crackling chicharon. Salty and airy, best dunked in spiced vinegar.

items.name: pork skin
items.note: with a thin layer of fat

steps.text: Scrape any hairs off the skin with a sharp knife and rinse it well.
Simmer the skin with the water, salt, bay leaves and peppercorns until soft enough to pierce easily.
Drain and let it cool until you can handle it. Lay it skin side down and scrape off all the soft fat with a spoon or knife, leaving just the skin.
Cut the skin into pieces about 5 cm (2 in) square. Lay them in one layer on a rack set over a baking sheet.
Dry in the oven at 95°C (200°F) until the pieces are hard, translucent and glassy all the way through, turning them once.
Let the dried skin cool. Mix the vinegar, garlic, chilies and salt for the dip.
Heat the oil in a deep, heavy pot to 190°C (375°F). Fry a few pieces at a time. They should puff and curl within a minute; scoop them out once the bubbling slows.
Drain on a rack, sprinkle with salt and serve with the spiced vinegar.

tips: Pieces that stay hard did not dry long enough. Use a deep pot only a third full of oil and keep a lid nearby, since the skins spatter as they puff. Dried, unfried skins keep for weeks in an airtight jar.

title: Nilagang mani
intro: Fresh peanuts boiled in their shells in salty water until soft and creamy. You crack them open one by one, still warm, and they taste a little like beans.

steps.text: Rinse the peanuts several times, rubbing them between your hands, until the water runs clear of soil.
Put them in a pot with the water and salt. Place a small plate on top to keep them under the water.
Bring to a boil, then simmer, covered, until the kernels are soft. Crack one open to check.
Turn off the heat and let the peanuts sit in the salty water so they soak up more flavor.
Drain and serve warm.

tips: Dried peanuts in the shell take longer than fresh ones, up to 90 minutes, so keep tasting. Keep leftovers in the fridge and eat within 3 days.

title: Nilagang mais
intro: Corn on the cob boiled in lightly salted water until tender and served hot, plain or rubbed with butter. White glutinous corn gives a chewy bite; yellow sweet corn is juicier and sweeter.

items.name: ears of corn
items.note: white glutinous corn (malagkit) or yellow sweet corn, husked

steps.text: Pull off the husks and silk. Cut long ears in half so they fit the pot.
Bring a large pot of water to a boil with the salt.
Add the corn and boil until the kernels are tender: about 10 minutes for sweet corn, 20 to 25 minutes for white glutinous corn.
Drain and serve hot, with butter for rubbing over if you like.

tips: Leave a couple of the inner husks in the pot while boiling; they add a little extra corn flavor.

title: Inihaw na mais
intro: Corn on the cob grilled over charcoal until smoky and charred in spots, brushed with margarine and salt as it cooks. Chewy, salty-sweet and best eaten straight off the grill.

items.name: ears of corn
items.note: white or yellow, husks pulled back or removed

steps.text: Pull the husks back and tie them together to make a handle, or remove them, and pull off the silk.
Mix the melted margarine with the salt and sugar.
Grill the corn over medium charcoal, turning every few minutes, until the kernels are tender and charred in spots. Brush with the margarine mixture several times as it cooks.
Brush once more and serve hot.

tips: White glutinous corn is firm and can take a while on the grill. Boil it for 10 minutes first, then grill until charred.

title: Corn in a cup
intro: Sweet corn kernels tossed hot with butter, a pinch of salt and sugar, and a shower of cheese, served in a cup with a spoon. Rich, sweet and salty, the way mall kiosks make it.

items.name: sweet corn kernels
items.note: cut from 4 to 5 ears, or frozen

steps.text: Bring a pot of water to a boil. Add the corn kernels and boil until tender.
Drain well and return the corn to the warm pot.
Add the butter, salt and sugar and stir until the butter melts and coats every kernel.
Spoon into cups, top with cheese and a little mayonnaise if you like, and serve hot.

tips: Canned whole-kernel corn works too: drain it and just heat it through with the butter.

title: Binatog
intro: Chewy, puffed white corn kernels topped with freshly grated coconut and a sprinkle of salt or sugar. Soft, slightly sweet and nutty, eaten warm from a cup.

items.name: dried white hominy corn
items.note: lime-treated white corn, sold as binatog corn or pozole

steps.text: Rinse the corn and soak it overnight in plenty of cold water.
Drain, put the corn in a large pot and cover with fresh water by 5 cm (2 in). Bring to a boil.
Simmer, partly covered, until the kernels burst open like flowers and are chewy-tender. Top up with hot water as needed so the corn stays covered.
Drain and toss with the salt while warm.
Spoon into cups and top with grated coconut. Let each person add more salt or sugar.

tips: For a quick version, rinse 2 cans of white hominy, simmer for 10 minutes and top as above. Grated coconut spoils fast, so add it just before serving.

title: Cornick
intro: Big corn kernels deep-fried until crunchy and tossed with salt and crisp fried garlic. A loud, salty snack that goes with a cold drink.

items.name: dried large white corn kernels
items.note: such as dried hominy or giant corn

steps.text: Soak the corn in plenty of water for 12 to 24 hours, until the kernels have swelled. Count this as advance prep.
Drain and spread the corn on towels. Pat and air-dry until the surface is completely dry, since wet kernels spatter hard.
Heat the oil in a deep, heavy pot to 160°C (320°F). Fry the garlic slices until light golden, then scoop them out onto paper towels.
Raise the oil to 175°C (350°F). Fry the corn in small batches with a splatter guard on, stirring now and then, until deep golden and crunchy.
Drain on a rack and toss right away with the salt, garlic powder and fried garlic.
Let cool completely; the kernels crisp up more as they cool.

tips: Kernels can pop out of the pot as they fry, so use a deep pot no more than a third full of oil and keep a lid or splatter guard on. Stored airtight, cornick keeps for a week.

title: Helmet
intro: Chicken heads simmered in soy and garlic, then grilled on skewers with a sweet barbecue glaze until the skin turns crisp. A crunchy, savory isaw stand favorite for adventurous eaters.

items.name: spiced vinegar
items.note: cane vinegar with chopped onion, garlic and chili

steps.text: Singe off any remaining pinfeathers over a flame and pull out what is left with tweezers. Cut off the beak tips with kitchen shears and rinse the heads well.
Simmer the heads with the water, soy sauce, vinegar, garlic, bay leaves and salt until the skin is tender.
Drain and let them cool, then thread 3 heads onto each skewer through the thickest part.
Mix the ketchup, soy sauce, brown sugar and oil for the baste.
Grill over medium-hot charcoal, turning and basting often, until glazed and crisp.
Serve hot with spiced vinegar.

tips: Ask your poultry seller for heads that are already cleaned. Simmer them a day ahead and grill just before serving.
